tldr: Magnette live-codes a 'dog' clone of cat to show that modern Java plus JBang, Picocli, GraalVM and TamboUI covers the jobs you currently write in Bash.
summary: Tired of forgetting Bash syntax twice a year, Magnette builds a 'dog' command that does what cat does. He runs it with plain `java Dog.java` (single-file source launch, there since JDK 11 via JEP 330), then splits it into helper classes in sub-packages with no Maven or Gradle layout, which the multi-file source launcher compiles in memory. Java 25's instance main methods remove the class and `public static void main(String[] args)`, the implicitly available `IO` class replaces the BufferedReader boilerplate for reading input, and a shebang line on an extensionless file lets the script live in your bin directory.

JBang adds what plain Java lacks: `//DEPS` lines with Gradle-style coordinates (he pulls in LangChain4j to prompt an LLM from a script), automatic JDK download for machines without Java, and `jbang export native` to build a GraalVM native image, with `//NATIVE_OPTIONS` to fix the reflection Jackson needs. `jbang init` with the CLI template generates a Picocli skeleton whose annotations produce help, version and typed options. He closes with TamboUI, a Java terminal UI library inspired by Rust's Ratatui, running a small game while Claude Code works, and an unreleased GraalVM feature that cut a 0.3-second script start-up sharply on second run.
keyPoints: `java File.java` has run single-file programs without javac since JDK 11; multi-file source launching handles helper classes in plain directories.
Java 25 makes `void main()` plus the `IO` class enough for a readable script; a shebang requires dropping the `.java` extension.
JBang reads dependencies, Java version, native-image and JVM options from comment lines at the top of the file and can install a JDK if none is present.
Native images of scripts using reflection-heavy libraries such as Jackson need reflection configuration, which JBang can pass in-file.
Picocli via `jbang init` gives a real CLI with generated help and typed options in a single file.
takeaways: Write your next throwaway automation as a single Java file run with `java` and a shebang instead of Bash.
Install JBang and use `//DEPS` when a script needs a library, rather than creating a Maven project.
Start CLI tools from the JBang Picocli template so help and argument parsing come for free.
Try `jbang export native` for scripts you run often and where JVM start-up matters.

quotes.text: All the code you don't write is the code without bugs.

watchIf: You still reach for Bash or Python for small automation jobs and would rather use the Java you write every day.
